[b]Islamist Violence in New Westmore has a New Name - Al-Qadi[/b]
[i]A report by the Westmorian Broadcasting Corporation[/i]

New Westmore is no stranger to religious violence. For many years, the nation has had to deal with violence between different religious groups within its borders, which normally manifests itself as knife crime, organised crime or even gun crime; the main culprits of this kind of violence are almost always Islam and Christianity, where clashes between its sects and even against each other are nothing new to authorities and commoners alike.

While this violence is serious, New Westmore's authorities have been relatively effective at putting an end to this kind of crime.

That is, until recently.

For the last 2 months, there has been a sudden uptick in religious violence, with its groundwork possibly being laid many months before. Much of this violence is perpetrated by Muslims, who have been indoctrinated by an entirely new underground movement that has rooted themselves into the Shaman-majority communities of Greater Brunswick and the Greater Dalesburg Area.

This movement goes by the name of Al-Qadi.

According to the Commissioner of the Internal Affairs Agency, Ali Rahmoud, Al-Qadi is the most recent incarnation of Islamism, and more specifically Kominism, within Westmore's Shaman community.

Islamism is a political and religious movement that advocates for greater Islamic influence in political structures, under the belief that such a system would be far superior than any other ideology or government type. It is often utilised by extremists, who use violent acts to further push the ideology and its message.

Within Westmore, Islamist ideology acts as the foundation of Kominism, a separatist political movement that advocates for the creation of a sovereign nation located on the lands of Greater Brunswick called Qamin, otherwise known as Komin. Its origins can be traced back to the mid-1940s, where the movement originally started as a protest movement against the brutal Whitemen Policy-led governments of the era. 

"Kominism never really underwent a major shift of any kind." Rahmoud told WBC during an interview. "From day one, it has always advocated for a sovereign nation, just for the Shamans of New Westmore. While back then it would have had some legitimacy, given the government did oppress Shamans to high hell and back, in the modern day, Kominism has no place in our society. Kominism is very much a product of its time, but the strangest thing is that it somehow adapted just enough for it to be at least appealing to some people to this day."

"Al-Qadi is a testament to Kominism's survival and adaptation with time."

The Al-Qadi has been linked to a number of violent crimes that have occurred throughout the north and the west of the nation, where most Shamans live. The brunt of these reported crimes are concentrated within Greater Brunswick, and more specifically Brunswick City.

"Al-Qadi is weird in the sense that it isn't actually a full-blown terrorist organisation, like say, the Sal-Baliz." Rahmoud spoke on the modus operandi of the Al-Qadi. "They operate more like a gang, or a mafia, but without the well-defined territory, the fronts or any of the bells and whistles associated with those kinds of crime cells."

"See, the Al-Qadi will often orchestrate a targeted attack that at first sight appears to be a hit commissioned by a gang. For example, they might attack a business by ramming a car through its front window. Gangs do that all the time, why suspect that it's anything more than a gang hit? From there, the only way you can tell that it is an act of political/religious violence by the fact that somewhere nearby, religious scripture, political slogans or iconography will be spray-painted on a wall."

"Another odd quirk about them is that they appear to be decentralised. Whoever is leading this operation doesn't actually live in Westmore themselves, if there even is a leader to begin with. Al-Qadi seems to be a sort of cloud of disgruntled Kominists and Islamists who are acting as one. Quite literally, their barrier of entry is so low that anyone could simply join their cause by engaging in their acts of political violence."

In recent times, Al-Qadi's attacks have ramped up in intensity.

On the 14th of Wednesday, a 7-hour siege that begun at 9am took place in Brunswick City's CBD. 3 armed gunmen holed themselves up in a store and took the occupants inside as hostages. During the siege, the gunmen demanded for the release of all Muslim prisoners in Westmore, and requested for an airplane to take them to Sal-Baliz. They initially threatened to kill one hostage for every hour their demands were not met; eventually, negotiators talked them down to wait until 6pm for their demands to be met.

At 5pm, Westmore National Guard soldiers stormed the store and apprehended the gunmen. One of the terrorists were shot and killed at the site. None of the hostages died. Later on, the two surviving terrorists identified themselves as part of the Al-Qadi.

The siege marks a concerning turning point for the Al-Qadi's future. Many believe that their attacks will continue to intensify, eventually resulting in full-blown terrorist attacks that may kill hundreds or even thousands.

There have been calls for the government to do more to try and find the leaders of the Al-Qadi. President Holt has pledged to put an end to the organisation's activities by the end of 2025.

Upon being asked if there was any evidence to support the allegations of the Al-Qadi being operated by foreign elements, Rahmoud had this to say:

"We have some evidence that seems to suggest Al-Qadi might be a foreign operation. However, it is too early to confirm it as fact."
